doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Playing sick to avoid Georgia; basic training at Camp Roberts
summary: A white sergeant helped him fake illness and get California orders; he never touched a saxophone during 14 weeks of training.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: He said, “You play sick, because you don’t want to go to Georgia. That’s the heart of the South. You don’t want to go down there.” So I actually for the first time in my life played sick. I was so convincing. He helped me along. He said, “Can’t you see he’s sick? He can’t be shipped out.” So they changed my orders. The next time orders came through for me to be shipped out, they came through for California. I said, California sounds better than Georgia. So I was shipped to California for basic training to a place called Camp Roberts, which was located about midway between San Francisco and Los Angeles. No army camp is a paradise, believe me. I liked the sound of California. I had never been there before, but Camp Roberts didn’t endear me to California, anymore than I had ever been before. Training was 14 weeks. It was rigorous, and during that entire time I never touched a saxophone.
Has there been another 14-week period in your life where you never touched one?
Never, not since I took it up. I didn’t perform for three months. That was the longest time I --
But that can’t be very tough on you. It’s just a saxophone.
Right, right, right. If I just didn’t use my right hand for three months, it wouldn’t affect me, right?
Is that a rhetorical answer to a rhetorical question?
